articles.summary: As the global energy transition accelerates, maintaining the long-term stamina of critical infrastructure like wind turbines requires being able to spot hidden risks before they can become failures. Proactively protecting these systems means uninterrupted energy for neighborhoods, smarter and safer environments for inspectors, and lower operational costs.
articles.title: Expert Vision: How a GE Vernova Engineer Uses AI to See the Invisible

articles.summary: When he was a teenager, Allen Millard’s design and technology class in England went on a field trip to a coal-fired power plant. The visit changed his life. “For someone who was 15 years old to see this great big power station with all these massive machines and huge amounts of complexity, it was really fascinating,” Millard recalls. “Yet it was run by ordinary people who were very approachable and could explain how everything worked. I thought, ‘This is where I want to be.’”
articles.title: Engineers of Change: The Next Generation of Problem Solvers Starts Here

articles.summary: For decades, steelmakers have fought to tame their electric arc furnaces, whose power demand fluctuates wildly as they work their way through a jagged, shifting pile of scrap metal. Now a strikingly similar electrical challenge is emerging at the front line of the AI boom at large-scale data centers, where electricity demand can swing by tens of megawatts (MW) in milliseconds, making it harder to keep the grid stable.
articles.title: How GE Vernova’s New Technology Is Managing Power Swings at AI Data Centers

articles.summary: Nuclear energy offers reliable, lower-carbon power, but building a traditional large reactor can mean massive capital costs and construction schedules that are too slow for meeting the growing demand for reliable, low-carbon power. How to overcome these obstacles was a problem that a team of engineers, led by Christer Dahlgren and Brian Hunt, were ruminating on 10 years ago at the company that is today known as GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy. As the team explored designs, Dahlgren pitched an idea that could dramatically simplify the overall design for a small modular reactor (SMR).
articles.title: The Whiteboard Idea Rewriting the Future of Nuclear Power

articles.summary: Nobody blinks when a decades-old office tower gets a facelift. New elevators, heating, and plumbing give the owner a high-performing, future-proof building at a fraction of the cost of building new — and eliminate much of the new construction red tape. Doing the same for another kind of skyscraper, an aging wind turbine, used to be far more rare. Owners could swap out aging parts for replacements, but they rarely changed the machine’s silhouette.
articles.title: Second Wind: This Squad Is Rejuvenating America’s Wind Turbine Fleets, Not Tearing Them Down

articles.summary: Building reliable power in the Amazon rainforest, one of the world’s most remote locations, takes more than just erecting towers and panels. Wind and solar don’t produce electricity 24/7, so grid operators are constantly juggling to maintain a steady, stable flow of energy. Overcoming those challenges is exactly what the new Azulão I thermal power plant in Brazil was built to do.
articles.title: Deep in the Amazon, a New Power Plant Aims to Deliver Grid Stability for Complex Transmission Networks
